questions.q: What does a Database Transaction Unit (DTU) bundle together?
options: Compute, memory, and I/O, blended into a single number
Only the number of concurrent connections allowed
questions.explain: The DTU model's simplicity comes from reducing sizing to one blended number covering compute, memory, and I/O.

questions.q: Why can't Azure Hybrid Benefit be applied to a DTU-based database, even if the organization owns SQL Server licenses?
options: Because DTU pricing doesn't separate compute cost from the bundle, and Hybrid Benefit specifically discounts the compute cost line item
Because Azure Hybrid Benefit doesn't exist as a real Azure feature
Because DTU-based databases can't run any SQL Server workloads
Because Hybrid Benefit only applies to Managed Instance, never Azure SQL Database
questions.explain: Hybrid Benefit needs a separate compute price to discount, which only the vCore model provides.

questions.q: What does the vCore model separate that the DTU model bundles together?
options: Compute and storage — each priced and sized independently
questions.explain: vCore lets you choose compute (vCores + generation) and storage independently, unlike DTU's blended bundle.

questions.q: Which service tiers exist only under the vCore model, with no DTU equivalent?
questions.explain: Any workload needing Business Critical or Hyperscale has already decided vCore, since DTU has no equivalent tiers.

questions.q: Per this lesson's decision guide, which model should a workload with no existing SQL Server license and a preference for the simplest sizing story choose?
options: The vCore model with Hybrid Benefit
questions.explain: Without a license to apply via Hybrid Benefit, the DTU model's one-number simplicity is the more direct fit.
